whatTheyArgued: Biology as found. Tungara (Engystomops/Physalaemus pustulosus) males call in choruses; females visit and choose among them by call features. The advertisement call is a whine, and males can add a facultative 'chuck'; the chuck makes the call more attractive to females (Ryan 2008, Animal Behaviour 76, read in full text). In dense choruses, search-result summaries of the literature (not read in full) report that other callers' whines overlap a male's chucks, overlap lowers attractiveness, and males respond by adding more chucks. So the documented competitor effect is on the MALE signaller (call escalation), not a change in a female's acceptance threshold. I found no source in what I read showing the female's threshold rises when a rival is present.

scholarship.ref: Santiago Ron (2008), 'The evolution of female mate choice for complex calls in tungara frogs', Animal Behaviour 76:1783-1794 (full text read)
scholarship.supports: choruses, female choice by call features, facultative chuck that enhances attractiveness; calls with and without chucks traditionally called complex and simple
scholarship.disputes: Ron questions the sensory-exploitation story for the chuck preference (ancestral-state reconstruction, sampling of Engystomops species); says nothing on competitor-dependent thresholds.

scholarship.ref: Chorus-size and chuck-overlap findings (Bernal/Ryan lineage), as summarized by search results and the arXiv model 'Modeling sexual selection in Tungara frog and rationality of mate choice'
scholarship.supports: males add chucks as chorus size rises because overlap reduces call attractiveness (summary only; the PDFs I fetched did not extract, so I did not read the papers' text)
scholarship.disputes: Not verified against the primary papers; treat as a lead, not a settled citation.

ourUse: contest.js: a scored-candidate frame with co-present competitors must clear a stricter margin (contestedMargin) than an uncontested one; co-presence raises the bar and never raises a score. The compendium puts the analogy in the female: 'a female's acceptance threshold rises when a competing male's call is in the frame'.

bends.ours: Compendium work: 'a female's acceptance threshold rises when a competing male's call is in the frame.'
bends.theirs: The effect the manifest itself names (and what I could find) is on males: they add chucks when a rival's call is present or chorus is dense. I found no verified claim that a female's acceptance threshold rises.

bends.ours: Header: call grows more complex 'only when a competing male is in the frame, raising the margin a rival must clear'.
bends.theirs: 'Only' is not shown in the sources read, and 'the margin a rival must clear' is our decision-theoretic framing. In the frog the chuck is a signal, with overlap and attractiveness as the mechanism.

bends.ours: The frog names a design rule for a stricter margin on a contested pronoun binding.
bends.theirs: Nothing of the frog's mechanism (acoustic overlap, female phonotaxis, chuck attractiveness) is implemented. The design stands on the Borodino measurement (88% of frames refused) in the contest.js header, not on the frog.

fix: compendium work: 'Tungara males add chucks to their whine when rivals are calling nearby; females prefer the chuck-bearing call. contest.js borrows the idea that rivals in the frame change what counts as a clear signal: a contested frame must clear a stricter margin. The margin rule is ours; no frog threshold is claimed.'
compendium credit: 'the tungara frog - rivals in the frame change what counts as a clear signal (analogy; margin rule ours).'
contest.js handle line: drop 'only' and 'raising the margin a rival must clear'; say males escalate their call when a rival is present.
